summary:
Count each character, then output characters by count from high to low, breaking ties by character
code. Sorting the (at most 62) distinct characters is already fast; bucketing them by count makes
the ordering linear without any comparison sort.

question.md:
Rearrange `s` so its most frequent character comes first (all its copies together), then the next
most frequent, and so on.

- **All copies stay together:** `tree` becomes `eert`, never `eret`.
- **Ties are fixed by character code**, so the output is unique: digits (`0`–`9`) come before
  uppercase (`A`–`Z`), which come before lowercase (`a`–`z`). `aAbb` → `bbAa`.
- **Only letters and digits**, so at most 62 different characters, all in ASCII. A 128-slot array
  can count them.
- **Size:** up to 10⁵ characters. The output has the same length.

think.md:
Take `s = "banana12b"`. Count: a×3, b×2, n×2, 1×1, 2×1. Now order them: a first (3). Then b and n
tie at 2; `b` has the smaller code, so `bb` then `nn`. Then `1` and `2` tie at 1; `1` first.
Result: `aaabbnn12`.

think.caption: Write each character as many times as it appears.

think.md:
Two separate jobs: **counting** (one pass) and **ordering** the distinct characters. The ordering
is where approaches differ. The number of distinct characters is tiny here (≤ 62), but it's worth
seeing the linear version too: since a count is between 1 and n, characters can be dropped into
buckets indexed by count.

approaches.title: Pick the most frequent remaining character, again and again

idea.md: Keep the distinct characters in code order. Repeatedly scan them, counting each with a pass over `s`, and take the one with the highest count (the first one found wins ties, which is the smallest code). Append it count times and remove it.

build: List the distinct characters in increasing code order.
While any remain: find the one with the largest count (strictly larger replaces, so ties keep the smaller code).
Append it count times; remove it from the list.

Write the winner as many times as it appears, then take it out of the running.

complexity.md: **Time O(σ² · n)** for σ distinct characters: σ rounds, each counting σ characters with an O(n) scan. With σ = 62 and n = 10⁵ that's ~4 × 10⁸. **Space O(σ).**

approaches.title: Count once, then sort the distinct characters

idea.md: One pass fills `count[c]` for each ASCII code. Collect the characters with a nonzero count and sort them by `(−count, code)`. Write each one `count` times.

build: Count every character into a 128-slot array.
Sort them: higher count first, then smaller code.

lines.text: `qsort`'s comparator can't see local variables, so the counts live in a file-level array. Higher count sorts first; equal counts fall back to the smaller code. Counts and codes are small, so subtracting is safe.
A slot per ASCII code (letters and digits are all below 128).

notes.c: Reset the shared counts first, since the function may be called more than once.

lines.text: Only characters that actually appear: at most 62 of them.
Order by count descending, then code ascending.

notes.python: Sorting by `(−count, code)` gives "high count first, then small code" with one key.

lines.text: Write each character `count` times, keeping copies together.

notes.c: Fill a new buffer and terminate it; the caller frees it.

complexity.md: **Time O(n + σ log σ):** a counting pass plus a sort of σ ≤ 62 items, effectively O(n). **Space O(σ)** besides the output.

steps.text: Sorted by count, ties by code: a b n 1 2.

walk.title: Count once, sort the distinct characters by (count high → low, code low → high), write them out.

limits.md:
With 62 possible characters this is as fast as anything in practice. The limit appears with a
large alphabet (any Unicode text): sorting σ distinct characters costs O(σ log σ). Because a
count is an integer from 1 to n, bucketing by count avoids the comparison sort entirely.

approaches.title: Buckets by count

idea.md:
Count the characters. Make buckets `1 … n`; visit characters in increasing code order and add
each to `bucket[count]`, so every bucket holds its characters already sorted by code. Then read
the buckets from `n` down to 1 and write each character `count` times.

build: For codes 0 … 127 with a nonzero count, append the code to `bucket[count]`.
For `k` from n down to 1, write every character in `bucket[k]` k times.

lines.text: Drop each character into the bucket for its count. Characters are visited in code order, so each bucket comes out sorted by code: the tie rule for free.

notes.c: Each bucket is a linked list stored in two arrays: `head[k]` is the first character with count k, `next[c]` the one after `c`. Walking codes from 127 down and pushing to the front leaves each list in increasing code order.

lines.text: Highest count first; within a bucket, smaller code first. Each character is written `k` times.

notes.c: Terminate it, free the bucket heads; the caller frees the result.

complexity.md: **Time O(n + σ):** counting, one pass over the alphabet, and n buckets to read. **Space O(n + σ)** for the buckets.

steps.text: Characters visited in code order land in bucket[count]: 1→12, 2→bn, 3→a.
Bucket 2: b, n → write each 2 times.

walk.title: Bucket characters by their count. Read buckets from the highest count down.

takeaways.md:
- "Order by frequency" = **count, then order the distinct items**. Do the counting exactly once.
- When the sort key is a small integer (a count between 1 and n), **bucket sort** beats comparison
  sorting.
- Visiting keys in their natural order while filling buckets makes ties come out in the right
  order without extra work.
